sentences.text: The eastern moa is the only species currently recognized within the genus Emeus, which belongs to the family Dinornithidae and the order Dinornithiformes.
This bird stood approximately 1.5 meters tall and weighed between 36 and 79 kilograms.
It possessed a long neck, large powerful legs with short strong tarsi, and beige hair-like feathers without vestigial wing bones.
The tarsometatarsus was restricted to motion in the parasagittal plane, the pelvic musculature was poorly adapted for running, and exceptionally wide feet made it a very slow creature.
Its eggs measured 17.9 by 13.4 centimeters and weighed 1.9 kilograms.
Analysis of DNA from bone material confirmed that females were 15-25% larger than males.
The species went extinct around the year 1400.
Richard Owen originally described the first specimens in 1846, initially placing them in the genus Dinornis before they were later reclassified into the distinct genus Emeus.
The genus Emeus was established by Reichenbach in 1852.
The animal lived exclusively on the South Island of New Zealand, inhabiting lowland forests, grasslands, dunelands, and shrublands.
During the Last Glacial Maximum, the eastern moa was confined to a single glacial refugium before its range expanded during the Holocene.
The fossil range of the genus Emeus spans from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene, approximately 0.129 to 0 million years ago.
Researchers have long suspected that previously described species Emeus huttonii and E. crassus were actually male and female variants of a single species.
